q: You have twelve features planned for your MVP. Which question best decides what stays in the first version?
options: Which of these features do our closest competitors already offer?
Which of these features could we build fastest with our current skills?
Would the test of our riskiest assumption still work without this one?
Which of these features would look most impressive in a demo?
why: The MVP exists to test your riskiest assumption. Anything the test doesn't need goes on the 'not yet' list, however useful it might be later.

q: You can't code, and you want to test whether small gyms will take class bookings through a shared link. What's the most sensible way to build the first version?
options: Use no-code tools and handle some steps by hand, so you can change things yourself.
Hire an agency to build a full app with accounts, payments and a dashboard.
Spend six months learning to code so you can build it properly yourself.
Wait until you find a technical co-founder before testing anything at all.
why: You want the fastest, cheapest working version that you can change yourself. A full agency build or months of learning would delay the test, and waiting for a co-founder could delay it indefinitely.

q: Your customers are independent bakery owners. Which launch plan is likely to teach you the most?
options: Post on Show HN, because it can send thousands of visitors in a single day.
Launch on Product Hunt and ask your friends to upvote it in the first hour.
Buy a large ad campaign so as many people as possible see it at once.
Message the bakers you interviewed and post in the local business groups they use.
why: The right audience matters more than a big one. Show HN and Product Hunt mostly reach tech-minded readers, and asking friends to upvote breaks many sites' rules.

q: Which launch post is most likely to get useful responses?
options: One that calls the product revolutionary and says it will change the industry.
One that says who it's for, what it can't do yet, and asks one specific question.
One that lists every feature you plan to build over the next year.
One that shares projected user numbers to suggest strong momentum.
why: Specific, honest posts invite help from the people you built the product for. Hype, long roadmaps and invented numbers make readers skeptical and don't tell you what you need to learn.

q: In launch week you get 2,000 visits and 300 sign-ups, but only 15 people complete the core action and 3 come back. What's the most useful reading?
options: The launch worked, so it's time to spend money on ads and scale up.
The idea has clearly failed and you should abandon it straight away.
Interest exists, but few people reach the value; talk to sign-ups to learn why.
The numbers are too small to mean anything, so it's best to ignore them.
why: Visits and sign-ups show curiosity, while activation and return use show value. The gap between them is your clearest lead, and conversations with people who signed up will help explain it.
